children: The S&P 500 is approaching a historically favorable stretch of the calendar, with midterm-election-year data showing October and November have delivered the strongest average returns late in the cycle. The pattern does not guarantee another rally in 2026, but it gives investors a seasonal tailwind to weigh against still-elevated valuations, monetary-policy uncertainty and economic growth risks.
Carson Group data covering S&P 500 monthly returns from 1950 through 2025 shows October has historically been the strongest month during midterm years.
The index has gained an average 3.0% in October, finishing higher 73.7% of the time. November follows closely with an average 2.7% advance and a positive return in 78.9% of midterm years.

That represents a sharp reversal from the weaker portion of the calendar. June has historically fallen 2.1% on average during midterm years and finished higher only 36.8% of the time, while September has declined an average 0.8% and risen in fewer than half of observations.

Carson Group Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick reiterated the seasonal setup this week, noting that October has historically ranked first and November second among months during midterm years. Carson has also pointed to the S&P 500's relatively calm recent trading and its ability to hold above important technical levels.
The backdrop is especially relevant as the U.S. approaches its November 2026 midterm elections, when all 435 House seats and roughly one-third of Senate seats are up for election.
Investors should treat seasonality as supporting evidence rather than a standalone market signal.
A stronger October-November stretch would carry more weight if accompanied by improving earnings expectations, healthy market breadth and continued technical support for the S&P 500.

The historical numbers are nonetheless notable: October and November have averaged a combined 5.7% gain in midterm years. But inflation, Federal Reserve policy, valuations and economic growth can easily overwhelm seasonal tendencies.
The key test is whether the market's fundamentals begin moving in the same direction as the calendar.

title: S&P 500 Enters Historically Strong Midterm Stretch
